initial_requirements: Small and medium businesses need Mashbot to manage their presence across multiple social networks through a consistent service. Staff should be able to connect external accounts, prepare campaigns, schedule content for simultaneous publication, manage contributor, approver, and publisher roles, respond to audience activity, and monitor keywords and campaign history. The service should reduce the effort required to coordinate marketing and customer engagement across changing platforms.

slots.key: Approval chain structure and escalation path
slots.value: One person drafts the content or response, another person reviews it, and someone with publishing rights sends it out; for campaigns, a contributor prepares the materials, an approver checks brand and compliance, and a publisher schedules or posts it; customer responses follow the same handoff so a message can be assigned, reviewed if needed, and answered without losing track of who did what. If content is rejected or flagged for a policy issue, it must not go out as-is; the team should be able to see exactly why it was blocked; the contributor and approver must be notified; a manager should be able to review it if there’s any question or an exception is possible; the item should stay in draft or needs revision status until it is fixed and sent back through approval. If publishing succeeds but a related piece like replies or ingestion fails, keep the core campaign running and mark the affected part as degraded rather than stopping everything; retry automatically for transient issues; escalate immediately if the failure persists, affects multiple accounts, or blocks a role needed for approval or publishing. An approval override is allowed without escalation only when the person has explicit authority for that account or campaign type, such as a designated publisher or manager acting within assigned limits. If the override goes beyond their authority, it requires a second approval from someone higher up or a documented exception process with a clear reason and timestamp, and the system should block the action until that extra approval is recorded unless an agreed emergency setting applies. When letting someone deviate from the standard campaign path, the system should also check whether the required approvals are missing, and if the deviation would bypass a required review it should block or require very explicit confirmation. slots.value: If the exception changes access across multiple accounts, affects a sensitive content class, or creates a new approval authority, it should be handled centrally for one consistent decision and audit trail. If a request only applies to one business unit but touches a sensitive content class or increases approval rights beyond the requester’s normal role, it should still go to central review; local teams can make the business case and recommend it, but central makes the final call. If the exception creates a pattern of risk or confusion, central should step in rather than just relying on the audit trail.

topics.topic_content: Keyword monitoring and campaign history access

slots.key: Keyword tracking scope and alerting behavior
slots.value: Monitor keywords to spot brand mentions, campaign performance, and customer issues early so the team can respond quickly and adjust content; surface the main response activity on each channel, keyword hits tied to the campaign, and highlight unusual patterns like a surge in mentions, a negative comment pattern, or a missed scheduled post. Routine noise should be grouped or suppressed, while important alerts should be escalated to the right role, especially if they affect an active campaign or a high-priority account. Users can review trends or comments, but only managers or approvers can adjust monitoring rules or mark items as resolved when there’s a customer or reputation issue. Operationally, unauthorized or unmanaged items are skipped entirely and should not notify anyone beyond maybe an internal error log; duplicate or too-late items can still be ingested for history but should skip alerting. Late or duplicate items may be kept for audit trail or manager review of patterns later, but they should not reopen the normal response workflow unless someone manually flags them. For content that cannot be shown in every region, Mashbot should respect account region settings and policy tags, and keyword alert details should only be surfaced to the roles and regions permitted to handle that content.

slots.key: Campaign history retention and search capabilities
slots.value: Use campaign history to review trends or comments, and preserve past campaigns, published posts, and comments or replies if they matter for reference so the team can pick up work without losing context; also keep a clear history of what was posted, approved, changed, and when it went live. Access should remain limited day to day to the brands or campaigns each person is assigned to, and users should not change historical records. Retention should mostly follow the client’s contract and any legal or compliance rules, since some customers will want a longer history for reporting and others won’t. Audit record access should be restricted to the same roles that can see the related brand or campaign, with admins or compliance users only if explicitly needed for oversight. If content is private, unauthorized, or otherwise sensitive, it should be masked or limited as much as possible while still keeping enough detail for the audit trail. If a message is tied to a consent restriction, legal hold, or regional limitation, it should be masked or hidden from unauthorized users and still logged for audit purposes.

slots.key: Approval override blocking until extra approval
slots.value: The system should block the action until the required second approval or documented exception is recorded, unless an agreed emergency setting applies; users should still be able to save the request as pending and notify the approver right away, then retry after approval without re-entering everything as long as the content and target account have not changed. If the content or target account changes before approval, the pending request should be invalidated rather than silently updated, because the approval was based on a specific version. The user should resubmit so the approver is reviewing the current state, and the system should show what changed and why the old request no longer applies. Minor non-material changes, like a typo fix, may be handled as a fresh review rule, but the preference is to be conservative. A request should be invalidated if a later change affects what was approved in a meaningful way, including the text, media, destination account, audience targeting, schedule, or any compliance-sensitive setting. Minor non-substantive edits that do not change the message or destination can continue without a fresh review, but when in doubt the preference is to require a new review, especially for regulated or high-risk accounts. Material fields are the ones that can change the meaning, reach, timing, or compliance risk of the post, such as text content, images or video, target account, audience, schedule, and campaign assignment. Cosmetic fields are spelling fixes, formatting, or other edits that don’t alter the message or destination. In a middle case where a request is limited to one business unit but touches a sensitive content class or expands approval rights, it should still go to central review; local teams can make the business case and recommend it, but central should make the final call. Central may approve it as a temporary exception with an expiration and audit record.

slots.key: Temporary exception duration and scope limits
slots.value: Must end immediately as soon as the original reason no longer exists, without waiting for the expiry date; if the approved person leaves or the campaign changes in a way that affects the basis for the exception, it should be treated the same way and require a fresh request rather than a renewal by default. Central should revoke the exception early if the person misuses the access, if there’s any sign of unauthorized publishing or approval activity, or if the scope starts drifting beyond the original account or campaign. It should stop immediately if the change alters who is allowed to publish, what content can go out, or which audience or account is covered. A fresh request is required if the campaign purpose changes, the approved person changes, or the exception would need broader rights than were originally approved. Minor scheduling shifts with the same people and the same content scope can remain within the existing exception.

If the exception creates a pattern of risk or confusion, central should step in rather than just relying on the audit trail.

slots.key: Preserve campaign history and content relationships during migration
slots.value: Successful migration should preserve business history so the team can pick up work without losing context, including past campaigns, published posts, comments or replies where they matter for reference, and the link between content, the account it belonged to, and who approved or published it.

slots.key: Exclude sensitive credentials from migration
slots.value: Sensitive data such as tokens or passwords should not be migrated as plain data; passwords must be excluded entirely, and tokens should be treated as a special-case manual step rather than migrated automatically. If a platform provides a usable authorization token, it should be vaulted securely, never shown in plain text, and the team should be clearly warned that credentials were handled separately. Mashbot should respect whatever consent and permission flow each platform requires, even if onboarding steps differ by network; if a platform only grants limited scopes, only the features allowed by those permissions should be enabled; if reauthorization has to be done manually later, that is acceptable as long as the user is clearly guided through it; and the system should make it obvious when an account is partially connected versus fully ready.

slots.key: Partial account connection visibility and restrictions
slots.value: When an account is only partially connected, users should be able to see the account status, which permissions are missing, and which campaigns or features will be affected. But if the missing scope touches the exact channel or action, Mashbot should block it rather than trying to work around it.

slots.key: External API interactions required for each network
slots.value: Support Facebook, Instagram, X, and LinkedIn initially for campaigns and customer interaction; also plan to support TikTok and possibly YouTube later. Differences should be made obvious up front when a campaign is being prepared so staff can adjust content before scheduling it. Brands may need multiple accounts on the same network for separate regional, product, or business unit presences. Account types that the network does not allow for publishing or replying, or that are read-only (for example, certain analytics or advertising-linked accounts), should be excluded from those actions, subject to platform API limits and safely supported permissions. An override is allowed without escalation only when the person has explicit authority for that account or campaign type, such as a designated publisher or manager acting within their assigned limits. If the override goes beyond their authority, it requires a second approval from someone higher up or a documented exception process with a clear reason and timestamp, and the system should block the action until that extra approval is recorded unless an agreed emergency setting applies. If someone has permission for the action, the content is already approved and safe to publish, and the target account or time window has no active restriction, it can be allowed; unusual but still acceptable actions should require extra confirmation; actions that would bypass policy, go to the wrong account, or violate a blackout or legal restriction should be blocked entirely.

slots.key: Protection of connected social account credentials
slots.value: Connected social accounts should be linked through the network’s own authorization/consent flow rather than collecting the user's direct login in Mashbot. The user approves what Mashbot can do, and Mashbot stores the resulting token or connection details. This is preferred for safety and because it is easier to manage when platforms change authentication rules.

slots.key: Keyword monitoring access scope and permissions
slots.value: Access to sensitive content should be based on both role and assignment: a person can only see it if their job needs it and they are tied to that account or campaign. Account-specific content should be limited to people assigned to that account unless there is a formal override. For sensitive work, role alone is not enough; the person should also be assigned to that account or campaign, or explicitly granted temporary access. A contributor might be able to draft more broadly, but approval and publishing require much tighter control and usually both the right role and direct assignment. If someone isn’t assigned, they may only view a limited version or request access, but they should not be able to publish just because their title fits. Mashbot should respect the account’s region settings and any policy tags on the message or campaign, so content only appears to people who are allowed to see it. If a message is tied to a consent restriction, legal hold, or regional limitation, it should be masked or hidden from unauthorized users and still logged for audit purposes. For keyword monitoring, it should only surface the alert details to the roles and regions that are permitted to handle that type of content, rather than showing it broadly to everyone.
